blocks.content: docker build is the command that actually turns a Dockerfile and a build context into a finished image. Knowing its common flags well saves real time in day-to-day work.

At minimum, docker build needs a build context (usually ., the current directory) and typically a -t flag to name and tag the resulting image, without a tag, the image is only reachable by its raw image ID.

blocks.alt: A tag makes the resulting image easy to reference later

blocks.content: Beyond -t, three flags come up constantly: -f to point at a Dockerfile that is not named Dockerfile or not in the context root, --build-arg to pass build-time variables (covered in depth later in this module), and --no-cache to force a completely clean rebuild.

blocks.alt: A small set of flags covers the vast majority of real usage

blocks.content: Many real projects keep multiple Dockerfiles, one for production, one for local development, and use -f to point at the right one explicitly, while the build context itself can still be a different directory entirely.

blocks.alt: A named Dockerfile for a specific purpose

blocks.content: By default, Docker's newer BuildKit-based builder shows a condensed, auto-updating progress view. Passing --progress=plain switches to the full, linear build log, most useful when debugging a build failure and you need to see every line of output in order.

blocks.alt: Plain progress mode for full, linear build logs

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: docker build turns a Dockerfile and a build context into an image, -t is what makes the result easy to reference afterward.
-f, --build-arg, and --no-cache cover the majority of flags you will reach for beyond the basic command.
